item.text:
**8B.3 Bottom Line**

Abiy Ahmed’s 2024 record shows **real but uneven mobilization** of the state. The strongest evidence is in **macroeconomic reform, select public-service delivery, digital ID, and some planning around displacement and education**. The weakest area is **security and political control**, where the state was also mobilized, but often through **emergency rule, loyalist security reshuffles, parallel coercive structures, and information control** rather than clean rule-based implementation.

**Positive Evidence**

- **The Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia: First Review Under the Extended Credit Facility Arrangement** — IMF, 2024-10-18, [URL](https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2024/10/18/pr-24383-ethiopia-imf-completes-the-1st-review-under-the-ecf-arrangement). Claim: Ethiopia met all quantitative performance criteria and most structural benchmarks, which is strong evidence that Abiy’s macro reform program was being translated into enforceable targets and followed through in practice. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

- **The National Bank of Ethiopia Announces the Launch of a New Monetary Policy Framework** — National Bank of Ethiopia, 2024-07-09, [URL](https://nbe.gov.et/nbe_news/the-national-bank-of-ethiopia-announces-the-launch-of-a-new-monetary-policy-framework/). Claim: the NBE shifted to an interest-rate-based framework, defined price stability as the priority, and laid out new operating tools and an interbank market, showing real institutional mobilization behind the reform agenda. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.2.

- **Energizing Ethiopia: New World Bank Program Expands Access to Electricity** — World Bank, 2024-04-03, [URL](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/04/03/energizing-afe-ethiopia-new-world-bank-program-expands-access-to-electricity). Claim: the government and World Bank launched a phased power-sector program to strengthen the grid, improve utility viability, and mobilize private participation, which is concrete evidence of program-to-institution translation. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.2.

- **Disclosable Restructuring Paper - Access to Distributed Electricity and Lighting in Ethiopia (ADELE) - P171742** — World Bank, 2024-08-16, [URL](https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099082124120033234). Claim: the project’s explicit objective was to improve government capacity to mobilize and manage public financial and human resources, especially in administration, finance, procurement, and core systems. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.2.

- **Ethiopia Digitizes 620 Public Service Institutions** — ENA English, 2024-06-13, [URL](https://www.ena.et/web/eng/w/eng_4597948). Claim: the government reported digitizing 620 public service institutions and expanding digital-skills initiatives, which is concrete evidence of bureaucratic modernization rather than rhetorical reform alone. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.2.

- **Ethiopia launches inclusive ID system for refugees, boosts access to national services** — UNHCR Africa, 2024-03-07, [URL](https://www.unhcr.org/africa/news/press-releases/ethiopia-launches-inclusive-id-system-refugees-boosts-access-national-services). Claim: the government, via RRS/NIDP/UNHCR, rolled out digital refugee IDs to improve access to services and formal permits, showing administrative capacity being used for inclusion and state coordination. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.2.

- **UN agencies and Ethiopian government launch Durable Solutions Strategy for internal displacement** — UNHCR, 2024-11-15, [URL](https://www.unhcr.org/news/announcements/un-agencies-and-ethiopian-government-launch-durable-solutions-strategy-internal). Claim: Ethiopia and UN agencies launched a government-led strategy for displacement solutions, linking governance, social services, livelihoods, and peacebuilding into a concrete implementation framework. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.2.

- **ICRC Impact in Ethiopia: January - June 2024 Bulletin** — International Committee of the Red Cross, 2024-09-13, [URL](https://www.icrc.org/en/article/ethiopia-bulletin-january-june-2024). Claim: the ICRC said it trained ENDF, police, militias, judges, and local authorities on IHL/IHRL, indicating that at least part of the coercive apparatus was being directed toward compliance and operational discipline. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.2.

**Negative Evidence**

- **Ethiopia intelligence head Temesgen approved as deputy prime minister** — Reuters via Yahoo News Canada, 2024-02-08, [URL](https://ca.news.yahoo.com/ethiopia-intelligence-head-temesgen-approved-070230642.html). Claim: Abiy elevated the intelligence chief and ruling-party vice president to deputy PM while moving another security insider to NISS chief, which looks like consolidation of a security inner circle rather than broad meritocratic mobilization. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

- **Details of State of Emergency Declared by Gov't of Ethiopia** — ENA English, 2024-11-03, [URL](https://www.ena.et/web/eng/w/en_30124). Claim: the proclamation centralized coercive authority under a State of Emergency Operation Command responsible to the prime minister and suspended judicial authority over enforcement, which is concrete regime-control mobilization rather than rule-bound governance. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

- **In Ethiopia, a secret committee orders killings and arrests to crush rebels** — Reuters via EHRC, 2024-02-27, [URL](https://ehrc.org/in-ethiopia-a-secret-committee-orders-killings-and-arrests-to-crush-rebels-reuters/). Claim: the EHRC head confirmed the existence of Koree Nageenyaa and said it interfered in the justice system with widespread rights violations, which points to parallel coercive governance outside ordinary institutions. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

- **Freedom on the Net 2024: Ethiopia** — Freedom House, 2024, [URL](https://freedomhouse.org/country/ethiopia/freedom-net/2024). Claim: authorities restricted internet access, used emergency powers against journalists, and deployed propaganda/manipulation tactics, showing state capacity being used to manage information and suppress scrutiny. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

- **Ethiopia’s Deepening Crackdown on Dissent** — Human Rights Watch, 2024-03-04, [URL](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/03/04/ethiopias-deepening-crackdown-dissent). Claim: arrests of opposition figures and journalists, plus reported disappearances and arbitrary detention, indicate that the security apparatus was mobilized heavily for repression rather than clean program execution. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

- **Ethiopia authorities must stop using state of emergency law to silence peaceful dissent** — Amnesty International, 2024-02-19, [URL](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/02/ethiopia-authorities-must-stop-using-state-of-emergency-law-to-silence-peaceful-dissent/). Claim: Amnesty said emergency powers were used for warrantless arrests, curfews, movement limits, and bans on assemblies, which shows mobilization of state force for coercive control rather than narrow public-safety administration. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

- **Ethiopia authorities suspend three rights groups** — Human Rights Watch, 2024-12-02, [URL](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/12/02/ethiopia-authorities-suspend-three-rights-groups). Claim: Abiy praised reforms like media freedom and NGO registration while the government suspended rights groups, which is strong evidence of selective punishment and a rhetoric-versus-practice gap in how the ruling network mobilized the state. IDs: 8B.3; also 8B.1, 8B.2.

**Search Gap**

I did not find a single 2024 public document that laid out one unified, all-of-government mobilization plan with complete line-item budgets, staffing rules, and timelines spanning the party, military, bureaucracy, and coalition. The evidence is strongest when read **sector by sector**: the macro/administrative side looks meaningfully mobilized, while the security side looks mobilized too, but often in a coercive and opaque way that weakens the case for effective, rule-based execution.
